bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1's audit log shows a breadth-first route search. One entry was tampered with by the rival lab.
bug_hunt.rules: Neighbours are taken in alphabetical order. A node enters the queue only the first time it is generated. The goal test is applied when a node is removed from the queue.

steps.text: Remove S from the front of the queue. New nodes: A, B. Queue: [A, B].
Remove A from the front of the queue. New nodes: C, D. Queue: [B, C, D].
Remove D from the back of the queue. New nodes: G. Queue: [B, C, G].
Remove B from the front of the queue. New nodes: E. Queue: [C, G, E].
Remove C from the front of the queue. New nodes: none. Queue: [G, E].
Remove G from the queue: goal test succeeds. Path: S-A-D-G.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: BFS uses a FIFO queue, so it must remove the oldest node (the front). Removing the newest node makes it behave like depth-first search and loses the shallowest-first guarantee.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Remove B from the front of the queue. New nodes: E. Queue: [C, D, E].
bug_hunt.concept: BFS = FIFO queue; expands level by level; shallowest goal for unit costs.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: What data structure does BFS use, and what changes if you swap it for a stack?

bug_hunt.story_intro: A second log entry from Ra-1's crawler, a depth-first search. Find the corrupted line.
bug_hunt.rules: Visit unvisited neighbours in alphabetical order. The stack is the current path from S. Goal test when a node is visited.

steps.text: Visit S. Stack (current path): [S].
Visit A. Stack (current path): [S, A].
Visit C. Stack (current path): [S, A, C].
Visit E. Stack (current path): [S, A, E].
Dead end at E: backtrack to A. Stack (current path): [S, A].
Visit D. Stack (current path): [S, A, D].
Visit G. Stack (current path): [S, A, D, G]. Goal test succeeds.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: The stack must hold the whole current path from S to the node just visited. Here C was silently dropped, so the path no longer matches the edges that were actually followed.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Visit E. Stack (current path): [S, A, C, E].
bug_hunt.concept: DFS keeps only the current path (memory linear in depth) and backtracks at dead ends.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: Why does DFS need so little memory compared with BFS?

bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1's planner re-ran a depth-limited search with growing limits. One iteration was edited.
bug_hunt.rules: Depth-limited DFS for limits 0, 1, 2, ... Children in alphabetical order. A node at the limit is tested but not expanded. Every visit counts, including repeats across iterations.

steps.text: Limit 0: visited [S]. Goal not found.
Limit 1: visited [S, A, B]. Goal not found.
Limit 2: visited [S, A, C, F, D, B, E]. Goal not found.
Limit 3: visited [S, A, C, F, D, B, E, G]. Goal found.
Finished at limit 3. Total visits across iterations: 19. Path: S-B-E-G.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: With limit 2 the search may visit nodes at depth 0, 1 and 2 only. F is at depth 3, so it cannot appear in this iteration.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Limit 2: visited [S, A, C, D, B, E]. Goal not found.
bug_hunt.concept: IDS = repeated depth-limited DFS; shallowest goal with linear memory.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: Why is the repeated work in IDS not as wasteful as it looks?

bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1's optimiser climbs a terrain of scores. Its log claims every move was steepest-ascent.
bug_hunt.rules: Steepest ascent: move to the HIGHEST neighbour, and only if it is strictly higher than the current state.

steps.text: At idx 4 (h=2): neighbours idx 3=4, idx 5=6. Move to idx 3 (h=4) as the steepest uphill move.
At idx 3 (h=4): neighbours idx 2=5, idx 4=2. Move to idx 2 (h=5).
At idx 2 (h=5): neighbours idx 1=6, idx 3=4. Move to idx 1 (h=6).
At idx 1 (h=6): neighbours idx 0=7, idx 2=5. Move to idx 0 (h=7).
At idx 0 (h=7): neighbours idx 1=6. No neighbour is strictly higher: stop.
Result: stopped at idx 0 (h=7), a local maximum. The global maximum is h=12 at idx 9.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: Both neighbours (idx 3 = 4 and idx 5 = 6) are higher than idx 4 (h=2). Steepest ascent must take the higher one, idx 5. Taking idx 3 sends the climb to a poor local maximum.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: At idx 4 (h=2): neighbours idx 3=4, idx 5=6. Move to idx 5 (h=6).
bug_hunt.concept: Steepest ascent is greedy: it takes the best neighbour but can still stop at a local maximum.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: Name two ways to escape a local maximum in hill climbing.

bug_hunt.story_intro: A delivery-route log from Ra-1, using straight-line estimates h. One expansion was falsified.
bug_hunt.rules: Greedy best-first: always expand the frontier node with the smallest h; ties alphabetical. A node enters the frontier only the first time it is generated. Goal test on expansion.

steps.text: Expand S (h=9, lowest h). New: A, B, C. Frontier: [B(5), A(6), C(7)].
Expand A (h=6) as the lowest-h node. New: D. Frontier: [D(2), B(5), C(7)].
Expand D (h=2, lowest h). New: X. Frontier: [X(1), B(5), C(7)].
Expand X (h=1, lowest h). New: none. Frontier: [B(5), C(7)].
Expand B (h=5, lowest h). New: none. Frontier: [C(7)].
Expand C (h=7, lowest h). New: G. Frontier: [G(0)].
Expand G (h=0): goal test succeeds. Path: S-C-G.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: After S the frontier is A(6), B(5), C(7). The lowest h is B(5), not A(6), so expanding A contradicts the strategy.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Expand B (h=5, lowest h). New: D. Frontier: [D(2), A(6), C(7)].
bug_hunt.concept: Greedy best-first orders the frontier by h(n) alone, ignoring the cost already paid.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: Is greedy best-first complete or optimal? Why or why not?

bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1 scheduled shared resources by colouring a map. Its log says the solution is valid.

problem.constraint: Adjacent regions must have different colours

bug_hunt.rules: Assign variables in the listed order, trying colours Red, Green, Blue and taking the first one that does not clash with an already-assigned neighbour.

steps.text: Assign WA = Red (assigned neighbours: none).
Assign NT = Green (assigned neighbours: WA=Red).
Assign SA = Blue (assigned neighbours: NT=Green, WA=Red).
Assign Q = Green (assigned neighbours: NT=Green, SA=Blue).
Assign NSW = Red (assigned neighbours: Q=Green, SA=Blue).
Assign V = Green (assigned neighbours: NSW=Red, SA=Blue).
Assign T = Red (assigned neighbours: none).
All 7 regions assigned: solution returned.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: Q is adjacent to NT, and NT is already Green. Q = Green breaks the constraint NT != Q. The first colour in the list that does not clash is Red.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Assign Q = Red: no assigned neighbour has Red. Assignment: WA=Red, NT=Green, SA=Blue, Q=Red.
bug_hunt.concept: Backtracking checks constraints as it assigns, so a violation should be caught immediately.

bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1's maintenance robot planned how to return a backup disk. Check its reasoning chain.

problem.start: Robot in Room 2; backup disk in Room 3
operators: Pickup: needs robot in the disk's room and hands empty
Putdown: needs robot holding the disk; leaves it in the robot's room

bug_hunt.rules: Work backwards from the difference: choose an operator that reduces it, then turn its unmet preconditions into sub-goals.

steps.text: Difference: the backup disk is in Room 3 but the goal is Room 1. The robot is in Room 2.
Operator that reduces the difference: Putdown while the robot is in Room 1.
Putdown has two preconditions: the robot holds the disk, and the robot is in Room 1.
Sub-goal 'robot holds the disk': Pickup, which needs the robot in Room 3 (where the disk is).
Sub-goal 'robot in Room 3': the robot is in Room 2, so Move(2->3) reduces that difference.
Final plan, in execution order: Pickup, Move(2->3), Move(3->1), Putdown.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: Pickup needs the robot to be in Room 3, but the robot starts in Room 2. The sub-goal Move(2->3) must be executed before Pickup.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Final plan, in execution order: Move(2->3), Pickup, Move(3->1), Putdown.
bug_hunt.concept: Means-end analysis picks operators that reduce the difference and recursively satisfies their preconditions.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: How does means-end analysis differ from forward state-space search?

bug_hunt.story_intro: Ra-1 reports success. Is its conclusion supported by its own trace?
bug_hunt.rules: Simple hill climbing: check the right neighbour first, then the left; move only to a strictly higher neighbour.

steps.text: At idx 0 (h=1): neighbours idx 1=2. Move to idx 1 (h=2).
At idx 1 (h=2): neighbours idx 0=1, idx 2=3. Move to idx 2 (h=3).
At idx 2 (h=3): neighbours idx 1=2, idx 3=4. Move to idx 3 (h=4).
At idx 3 (h=4): neighbours idx 2=3, idx 4=6. Move to idx 4 (h=6).
At idx 4 (h=6): neighbours idx 3=4, idx 5=6. No neighbour is strictly higher: stop.
Result: stopped at idx 4 (h=6). This is the global maximum, so the search is complete.

bug_hunt.why_wrong: Equal-height neighbours are not strictly higher, so the climb stops on a flat shoulder (idx 4 to 7). Taller ground exists at idx 9 (h=10), so this is not the global maximum.
bug_hunt.corrected_step: Result: stopped at idx 4 (h=6). This is a plateau (flat shoulder), not a peak. Global maximum is h=10 at idx 9.
bug_hunt.concept: Plateau: flat region where greedy moves stall; fixes include sideways moves (with a cap) and random restarts.
bug_hunt.viva_followup: What does allowing a limited number of sideways moves change here?

interrogation.story_intro: The rival lab posted a fake witness to the night of the tampering. Two chat windows are open. One is a human on the lab's night shift, the other is a bot.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: What is 4,873 x 6,291? Answer as fast as you can.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Ha, no chance in my head. Somewhere around thirty million? Give me a calculator.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: What did you have for breakfast?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Cold coffee and half a samosa. The canteen ran out of idli again.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: Just toast and tea. Breakfast is the most important meal of the day, so I never skip it!

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Tell me about a time the lab network went down.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Last March, mid-demo. Someone had kicked the switch under the desk. We all just stood there in silence.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: Network outages can be frustrating. A good approach is to restart the router and check all the cables.

tells: Instant, exact multiplication that no person does in their head
A generic slogan instead of a personal detail
Textbook advice instead of a lived story
interrogation.verdict: B is the bot. Passing the basic Turing Test means answering like a person over text only, so a perfect calculator reply is a giveaway.

concept_check.question: The interrogator and the suspects communicate only by typed text. Which test is this?
concept_check.explanation: The basic Turing Test is text-only. It needs natural language processing, knowledge representation, automated reasoning and machine learning, but no vision or robotics.

interrogation.viva_followup: Which four capabilities must a program have to pass the basic Turing Test?

interrogation.story_intro: The second witness claims to have been physically in the server room. This interview includes a video feed and a hatch for passing objects.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: I'm holding something up to the camera. What is it?

transcript.speaker: stage
transcript.text: [Video: a paper aeroplane with one crooked wing]

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: It looks like a folded document.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: A paper plane. Left wing is bent, so it'll veer off.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Please pass the red marker through the hatch. Cap off.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Of course, one moment.

transcript.speaker: stage
transcript.text: [30 seconds pass. Nothing comes through the hatch from A.]

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: Here you go.

transcript.speaker: stage
transcript.text: [A red marker, cap off, slides through B's hatch.]

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Which of you was at the server rack that night?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: I was there from about nine, checking the rack.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: Not me. I was in the lab on the second floor.

tells: Described the aeroplane only vaguely as 'a folded document'
Said it would pass the marker but never did
Fluent text that cannot back up its claim of being at the rack
interrogation.verdict: A is the bot. It handled the text but failed the two tasks that need a camera and a body.

concept_check.question: Which two capabilities does the Total Turing Test add to the basic test?
concept_check.explanation: The Total Turing Test adds a video signal (needing computer vision) and the chance to pass physical objects (needing robotics).

interrogation.viva_followup: Why might a text-only Turing Test be considered too narrow?

interrogation.story_intro: Two staff members describe their shift on the night Ra-1 was corrupted. One is a bot with a prepared story. Listen for consistency.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: What time did you start work that day?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Around ten. I do late shifts, so I'm never in before noon.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: I work nights, so I'm never in the building before six in the evening.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Who else was around?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Just Priya from QA, she was finishing a test run.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: The whole morning team was there. Priya from QA was at the next desk.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: So what did you see when you arrived?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: The lights were on in the lab and Priya's screen was open on the logs.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: When I got in at nine, the corridor was empty and the access panel was blinking.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Earlier you said you are never in before six in the evening.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: That is correct. I am never in before six in the evening. I arrived at nine in the morning.

tells: B stated a fact (never in before six in the evening) and later contradicted it
B kept both statements without noticing the conflict
A's account stayed consistent from start to finish
interrogation.verdict: B is the bot. It did not store and reason over what it had already said.

concept_check.question: Which capability does B's contradiction most directly show to be missing or weak?
concept_check.explanation: To stay consistent a system must store what it has been told or has said (knowledge representation) and use it to draw conclusions (automated reasoning).

interrogation.viva_followup: What does the knowledge representation component of an intelligent agent do?

interrogation.story_intro: The rival lab's bot was told to 'look human'. It was tuned to make typing mistakes. Compare the quality of the mistakes, not just the answers.

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: In one sentence, why did Ra-1 fail its safety check?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Its reward was wrong, so it optimised the wrong thing. Sorry, ugly sentence, but that's basically it.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: Its performance meassure rewarded speed over safety, so it chose fast actions.

transcript.speaker: stage
transcript.text: [Reply times: A took 11 seconds. B took 2 seconds.]

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: And what should the measure have rewarded?

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: Safe completions, honestly. Hmm, and it should punish shortcuts. I'd have to check the spec to be precise.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: The measure should have rewarded safty and correct task completion, not just throughput.

transcript.speaker: stage
transcript.text: [Reply times: A took 19 seconds. B took 2 seconds.]

transcript.speaker: Interrogator
transcript.text: Last one. Give me the spelling of 'necessary'.

transcript.speaker: A
transcript.text: n-e-c-e-s-s-a-r-y. I always have to stop and count the s's.

transcript.speaker: B
transcript.text: n-e-c-e-s-s-a-r-y. My typing is not always acurate.

tells: Exactly one typo per message, always in the fourth word or later 'technical' term
Perfectly spelled the word it was asked to spell, so its mistakes are for show
Replies arrive in exactly 2 seconds no matter how hard the question is
interrogation.verdict: B is the bot. It imitates human flaws on purpose, which is a good way to act humanly but not how a system acts rationally.

concept_check.question: B was built to imitate human behaviour, including faking typos. Which of the four approaches to AI does that follow?
concept_check.explanation: Imitating human behaviour so that people cannot tell the difference is the acting-humanly (Turing Test) approach. A rational agent would simply aim to maximise its performance measure, with no reason to fake mistakes.

interrogation.viva_followup: Why is acting rationally a more general goal than acting humanly?
